---
title: "Staged pipelines and missing units"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.align = "center")
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(cohortflow)
```

Real eligibility rarely happens in one pass over one tidy table. This
article covers three situations the basic workflow doesn't:

1. **Units that never appear in the data.** Someone was invited but has no
   record, so they are silently missing from the denominator.
2. **Eligibility assessed in stages.** Some criteria can only be checked
   after data is collected later, such as an outcome or a processed
   measurement.
3. **Looking at the cohort part-way through**, or keeping every row with a
   flag instead of filtering.

## Units with no record: `cf_expected()`

`apply_criteria()` starts from the rows in your data. A unit with no row at
all, such as an invited participant who never returned a form or a
scheduled visit that was never logged, is not counted anywhere. Often that
is the largest loss in the study, and it is invisible.

`cf_expected()` lists the units that *should* exist. Passed as `expected`,
it is joined to the data before any step runs, so missing units appear as
empty rows that the first step can count.

Here 220 people were invited, but the data has records for only 200:

```{r}
dat <- mock_parallel_rct(n_participants = 200, seed = 5)
invited <- cf_expected(participant_id = sprintf("P%04d", 1:220))

crit <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ !is.na(arm), label = "Record received") |>
  include(~ eligible_screen, label = "Passed screening") |>
  include(~ !is.na(consent_date), label = "Consented")

flow <- apply_criteria(dat, crit, id = "participant_id",
                       expected = invited, by = "participant_id")
flow
```

`apply_criteria()` reports how many expected units had no match. If that
number is unexpectedly large, the join key is usually at fault (for example
`"P0001"` against `"1"`), not the data collection.

`cf_expected()` builds every combination of its arguments, which suits
repeated measures. For example, every participant at every scheduled
visit:

```{r}
cf_expected(participant_id = c("P0001", "P0002"),
            visit = c("baseline", "6 weeks", "12 weeks"))
```

The first step should test a column that every real record has, so that
"no record" is counted on its own line rather than mixed into a later step.

## Eligibility in stages: `continue_criteria()`

Suppose screening and consent are assessed first, then outcome data is
collected for those who passed, and the final criteria depend on that new
data. Running `apply_criteria()` a second time on the survivors would start
the counts again from the reduced cohort: the second table's denominator
would leave out every stage-one loss, and the diagram would show only half
the study.

`continue_criteria()` instead adds steps to the existing flow, optionally
joining new columns first. The step numbers continue on, and the tables and
diagram show the whole study.

```{r}
stage1 <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ eligible_screen, label = "Passed screening") |>
  include(~ !is.na(consent_date), label = "Consented")

flow1 <- apply_criteria(dat, stage1, id = "participant_id")

# Later: follow-up data for those still in the study
set.seed(1)
followup <- data.frame(
  participant_id = cohort(flow1)$participant_id,
  weeks_followed = round(rnorm(nrow(cohort(flow1)), mean = 12, sd = 3)),
  outcome_recorded = runif(nrow(cohort(flow1))) > 0.1
)

stage2 <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ outcome_recorded, label = "Outcome recorded") |>
  include(~ weeks_followed >= 8, label = "Followed up for 8 weeks or more")

flow2 <- continue_criteria(flow1, stage2, join = followup, by = "participant_id")
flow2
```

```{r, fig.width = 6.6, fig.height = 4.6, fig.alt = "CONSORT diagram covering both stages: 200 assessed, then screening, consent, outcome recorded and follow-up steps in one cascade."}
as_consort_diagram(flow2, wrap_width = 30)
```

The new columns are joined onto *every* original row, so rows excluded at
stage one have `NA` there. That is correct: those values were never
measured for them.

Two mistakes are caught before any step runs:

```{r, error = TRUE}
# The stage-two columns were never joined
continue_criteria(flow1, stage2)

# The join has two rows for one participant, which would duplicate them
dup <- rbind(followup[1, ], followup)
continue_criteria(flow1, stage2, join = dup, by = "participant_id")
```

The combined pipeline is stored in the flow, so `export_criteria()` writes
both stages:

```{r}
length(flow2$criteria)
```

## The cohort at any step

`cohort()` and `excluded()` take a step selector, meaning "up to and
including this step":

```{r}
nrow(cohort(flow2, at = 0))            # step 0 is the starting data
nrow(cohort(flow2, at = "Consented"))  # after stage one
nrow(cohort(flow2))                    # the final cohort
```

`at` accepts a step number, a step label or a category name (meaning that
category's last step). If a string could mean either a label or a category,
use `label =` or `category =` explicitly.

`excluded()` returns everyone removed up to the chosen step, with the step
that removed them. Add `only = TRUE` for just the rows removed *at* that
step:

```{r}
excluded(flow2, at = "Outcome recorded", only = TRUE)[, c("participant_id", "cf_step", "cf_label")]
```

## Flags instead of filtering

Sometimes downstream code needs every row, for example to plot a complete
recording or to compare everyone assessed with the analysed cohort.
`cohort(flag = TRUE)` returns all rows in their original order, with columns
saying whether each was included and, if not, which step removed it:

```{r}
flagged <- cohort(flow2, flag = TRUE)
flagged[, c("participant_id", "cf_included", "cf_excluded_step", "cf_excluded_label")]
```

Combined with a step selector, the flags only consider steps up to that
point, so `cohort(flow2, flag = TRUE, at = "Consented")` marks who was still
in after stage one.
